ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The experiments were approved by the ethics committee at the University of XXX.

Participants completed the study in either their native or foreign language, allowing us to examine the Foreign Language Effect on judgments of both language-rich content (songs with lyrics) and language-poor content (paintings).
Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Polish, N=36) or a foreign language (English, N=42).

A total of 161 additional participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=17), hearing or visual impairments (N=3), and "inattentive" responding (N=141).
Participants were classified as "inattentive" if they failed to listen to the entire duration of more than one song.
Each song snippet was about one minute long, and participants were instructed to listen to the complete snippet before submitting their ratings.
Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Dutch, N=31) or a foreign language (English, N=26).
Additional 39 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=2), hearing or visual impairments (N=2), and inattentive responding (N=35).
Participants gave higher ratings to pieces of art they recognized, which fits with earlier research showing that people often prefer familiar art (Cutting, 2003).
table.formatted: Participants gave higher ratings to pieces of art they recognized, which fits with earlier research showing that people often prefer familiar art <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cutting, 2003)</ref>.

table.text: Half of the participants were native Dutch speakers (N=109), and the other half were native Polish speakers (N=101).

An additional 35 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=5), hearing or visual impairments (N=4), and inattentive responding (N=26).
Participants were assigned to the version of the experiment corresponding to their language pair (Polish-English or Dutch-English).

Additional 233 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=24), hearing or visual impairments (N=7), and inattentive responding (N=202).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants completed the study in either their native or foreign language, allowing us to examine the Foreign Language Effect on judgments of both language-rich content (songs with lyrics) and language-poor content (paintings).

> Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Polish, N=36) or a foreign language (English, N=42).

> A total of 161 additional participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=17), hearing or visual impairments (N=3), and "inattentive" responding (N=141).

> Participants were classified as "inattentive" if they failed to listen to the entire duration of more than one song.

> Each song snippet was about one minute long, and participants were instructed to listen to the complete snippet before submitting their ratings.

> Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Dutch, N=31) or a foreign language (English, N=26).

> Additional 39 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=2), hearing or visual impairments (N=2), and inattentive responding (N=35).

> Participants gave higher ratings to pieces of art they recognized, which fits with earlier research showing that people often prefer familiar art (Cutting, 2003).

> Half of the participants were native Dutch speakers (N=109), and the other half were native Polish speakers (N=101).

> An additional 35 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=5), hearing or visual impairments (N=4), and inattentive responding (N=26).

> Participants were assigned to the version of the experiment corresponding to their language pair (Polish-English or Dutch-English).

> Additional 233 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=24), hearing or visual impairments (N=7), and inattentive responding (N=202).

Ethics approval statement:

> The experiments were approved by the ethics committee at the University of XXX.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Perception of art in FL
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Perception of art is affected by the use of the foreign language.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Participants will be evaluating art (visual and music) using a 7-point Likert scale. They will rate the following aspects: profundity; quality; willingness to share/recommend and familiarity with the piece.
Each of the participants will be presented with 4 abstract-art paintings and 4 songs randomly selected for each participant from the larger pool of the n = 8 preselected pieces from each category.
table.study_design_overview: Participants will be presented with stimuli and will provide their judgments using either their native (Polish) or foreign (English) language. Songs are performed by the same artist in these two languages, and the songs have been preselected in terms of their familiarity, i.e., that both versions of a song are similarly familiar to participants.
table.statistical_tests:
We will conduct a linear mixed effects regression analysis, predicting averaged ratings of quality of the art, predicted by language (native vs foreign) and type of art (music vs visual), with additional control of L2 proficiency, gender, and familiarity with a piece.

We will repeat the preregistered analysis without any exclusions, serving as a robustness check.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will collect self-rated proficiency ratings (1-10), removing participants below 5. 
We will exclude trials with songs on which participants spent less than the duration of the piece. We will discard entire data from an participant, if they more than once spent less time listening to a song than its duration. 
We will also exclude data from participants with hearing or visual impairment.
table.sample_size: We intend to collect as many participants as possible given the time available by Research Assistants. The target sample is 300 participants prior to exclusions by proficiency.
table.additional_comments: We will repeat the preregistered analysis without any exclusions, serving as a robustness check.

table.title: Perception of songs in FL
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Perception of songs is affected by the use of the foreign language (makes the songs seem more profound/likeable/of a better quality in the Foreign Language).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Participants will be evaluating art (music) using a 7-point Likert scale. They will rate the following aspects: profundity; quality; willingness to share/recommend and familiarity with the piece.
Each of the participants will be presented with 8 preselected songs.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be presented with stimuli and will provide their judgments using their native and foreign language (within subject). Songs are performed by the same artist in both languages, and they have been preselected in terms of their familiarity, i.e., both versions of a song are similarly familiar to participants. Participants will see 4 songs in their native language, and 4 different songs in their foreign language.

There will be two samples:
a) Polish people
b) Dutch people

Both of the above will see half of the materials in their native language (Polish/Dutch) and half of the materials in their foreign language (English).
table.statistical_tests:
First we will run a correlation check on all of the DVs. If they achieve r of at least .7, we will average them and use the averaged score of the quality of the song to use in an exploratory model. We will conduct a mixed model analysis:

Main interest:

Model (M) 1.1 
dependent variable: profoundness score
factors: language (native/foreign) - simple coded (-.5, .5)
covariates: 
clusters: Participants' ID, Item number

M1.2 - addition of familiarity (1-7) covariate,
M1.3 - addition of proficiency (1-10) covariate

Exploratory analyses:
We will follow the same modelling but for different DVs:
M2.1, 2.2, 2.3 - DV - liking score
M3.1, 3.2, 3.3 - DV - recommendation score

And if the all three DVs correlation r is >.7
M4.1, 4.2, 4.3 - DV - quality of the song score
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will collect self-rated proficiency ratings (1-10), removing participants below 5.
We will exclude trials with songs on which participants spent less than the duration of the piece. We will discard entire data from an participant, if they more than once spent less time listening to a song than its duration.
We will also exclude data from participants with hearing or visual impairment.
table.sample_size: The target sample is 200 participants after exclusions (proficiency, and attention checks) - 100 per language pair.
table.additional_comments: There were two similar, separate previous studies on the topic conducted some time ago. This study comes with a design change and a new set of data and participants.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------

"p<.05", "p<.05", "p<.05", "p<.05"), Text = c("Adding familiarity (M2) revealed a significant effect: more familiar pieces were rated as more profound (B=0.19, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35], p<.05).", 
"The proficiency model (M3) found a significant three-way interaction between proficiency, language, and type of art (B=0.40, 95% CI [-0.71, -0.09], p<.05).", 
"The base model (M1) showed a significant main effect of type of art (B=0.69, 95% CI [0.06, 1.33], p < .05), with music rated higher than paintings.", 
"When for the model was extended by familiarity ratings (M2), we found that familiar pieces were rated higher for profoundness (B=0.15, 95% CI [0.02, 0.27], p<.05).", 
"When introducing proficiency instead of familiarity in the model (M3), we observed a significant main effect of type of art (B=0.74, 95% CI [0.11, 1.38], p<.05), with music rated higher than paintings.", 
"The model also revealed a significant three-way interaction between proficiency, language, and type of art (B=0.47, 95% CI [0.04, 0.91], p<.05).", 
"M1 showed a significant main effect of art type (B=0.70, 95% CI [0.16, 1.24], p<.05), with music rated as more profound than paintings.", 
"M3 confirmed that language proficiency also had no significant effect, while art type remained significant (B=0.71, 95% CI [0.17, 1.25], p<.05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)

This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 24 codebook/README/label sources and 3376 data columns across 66 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (32 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 17% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `Filter 1`, `Filter 2`, `Filter 3` while the data has `Filter 1`, `Filter 2`, `Filter 3`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

Instructie

Om de liedjes te beluisteren heeft u oortjes of een koptelefoon nodig en dient u in een stille ruimte te zijn. Heeft u deze bij de hand en is dit het geval? Klik dan op 'Begin de studie'. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 3376 columns across 66 data files.
#### Issues Identified

588 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 66 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  3 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  0 of 3 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  3 installable dependencies detected.
- 6852 statistics stored from the extracted output; 25 of 36 reported tests matched (69.4%).

live_data_statements: Participants completed the study in either their native or foreign language, allowing us to examine the Foreign Language Effect on judgments of both language-rich content (songs with lyrics) and language-poor content (paintings).
Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Polish, N=36) or a foreign language (English, N=42).

A total of 161 additional participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=17), hearing or visual impairments (N=3), and "inattentive" responding (N=141).
Participants were classified as "inattentive" if they failed to listen to the entire duration of more than one song.
Each song snippet was about one minute long, and participants were instructed to listen to the complete snippet before submitting their ratings.
Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Dutch, N=31) or a foreign language (English, N=26).
Additional 39 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=2), hearing or visual impairments (N=2), and inattentive responding (N=35).
Participants gave higher ratings to pieces of art they recognized, which fits with earlier research showing that people often prefer familiar art (Cutting, 2003).
Half of the participants were native Dutch speakers (N=109), and the other half were native Polish speakers (N=101).

An additional 35 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=5), hearing or visual impairments (N=4), and inattentive responding (N=26).
Participants were assigned to the version of the experiment corresponding to their language pair (Polish-English or Dutch-English).

Additional 233 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=24), hearing or visual impairments (N=7), and inattentive responding (N=202).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("Exp1aICC.R", "Exp1bICC.R", 
"Exp2ICC.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Exp1aICC.R", "Exp1bICC.R", "Exp2ICC.R"
), Outcome = c("errored", "errored", "errored"), Detail = c("undefined_variable", 
"undefined_variable", "undefined_variable"), "Time (s)" = c(1.9, 
1.9, 1.9)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).
**Calls that install packages in the code**

9 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

#### Duplicate files across repo mirrors

3 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: `Exp1aICC.R` at `https://osf.io/download/9y3rd/` (same as `Exp1aICC.R` at `https://osf.io/download/9y3rd/?view_only=0b48e990d6c54c3ea40a24ec9c3c8049`); `Exp1bICC.R` at `https://osf.io/download/zja9f/` (same as `Exp1bICC.R` at `https://osf.io/download/zja9f/?view_only=0b48e990d6c54c3ea40a24ec9c3c8049`); `Exp2ICC.R` at `https://osf.io/download/375fd/` (same as `Exp2ICC.R` at `https://osf.io/download/375fd/?view_only=0b48e990d6c54c3ea40a24ec9c3c8049`).
#### Reported vs. reproduced
36 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 25 matched (25 fully, 0 partially) — 69.4% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

info.title: Using a Foreign Language Does Not Make the Art More Profound -Familiarity Does

author.affiliation:
Institute of English Studies
								Faculty of Languages, Literatures, and Cultures
								University of Wroclaw

Institute of English Studies
								Faculty of Languages, Literatures, and Cultures
								University of Wroclaw

Centre for Language Studies
								Radboud University

Institute of Psychology
								Faculty of Historical and Pedagogical Sciences
								University of Wroclaw

text.text: This study investigated whether using a foreign language affects aesthetic judgments of art.
Across three experiments (N=345), Polish-English and Dutch-English bilinguals rated songs and paintings on profoundness, liking, recommendation, and familiarity.

Participants completed the study in either their native or foreign language, allowing us to examine the Foreign Language Effect on judgments of both language-rich content (songs with lyrics) and language-poor content (paintings).
Contrary to theoretical predictions based on reduced emotional engagement and impaired metacognition in foreign languages, presentation language did not significantly affect any ratings.
Instead, two factors consistently predicted profoundness judgments: familiarity and medium.
Participants rated familiar artworks as more profound regardless of language condition, and music received higher profoundness ratings than paintings across all experiments.

These findings suggest that aesthetic perception is primarily driven by prior exposure and medium-specific characteristics rather than the language in which art is encountered, challenging assumptions about linguistic effects on aesthetic judgments.
The meaning of art is not an affordance.
Instead, just like any other act of perception, it is created by its recipients.

While doing so, recipients consider various information about the piece itself (e.g., topic, technique, colours) and its externalities (e.g., artist, cultural background, social or historical context) (Pelowski et al., 2017).
text.formatted: While doing so, recipients consider various information about the piece itself (e.g., topic, technique, colours) and its externalities (e.g., artist, cultural background, social or historical context) <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Pelowski et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: They also consider information that should not be central, e.g., pseudo-profound descriptions or titles of a piece with only an impressive form but no real meaning (Turpin et al., 2019; Urbanek et al., 2024).
text.formatted: They also consider information that should not be central, e.g., pseudo-profound descriptions or titles of a piece with only an impressive form but no real meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Turpin et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Urbanek et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Traits and current states such as mood, attitudes, knowledge, and stereotypes affect how art is perceived and interpreted (Pelowski et al., 2016)-finally, people like what they already know.
text.formatted: Traits and current states such as mood, attitudes, knowledge, and stereotypes affect how art is perceived and interpreted <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Pelowski et al., 2016)</ref>-finally, people like what they already know.

text.text: Thus, familiarity with a piece helps to perceive it as of better quality (Cutting, 2003).
text.formatted: Thus, familiarity with a piece helps to perceive it as of better quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cutting, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In sum, more than the piece of art itself matters when judging it.
In the present study, we ask whether using a foreign language can affect how we perceive art.
Consider the experience of listening to songs like Umbrella by Rihanna (for non-English speakers) or Macarena (for non-Spanish speakers).
Even when the lyrics are understood, hearing them in a foreign language can make repetitive or simplistic content easier to ignore.
The songs often feel more tolerable than in one's native language.
This idea has not been formally tested, but it fits what we, and likely many others, have experienced.
Consistent with this introspective experience, experimental evidence suggests that using a foreign language can change how people perceive and evaluate art (e.g., Stephan et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Consistent with this introspective experience, experimental evidence suggests that using a foreign language can change how people perceive and evaluate art (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Stephan et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This idea is supported by studies on the Foreign Language Effect (Białek et al., 2020; Circi et al., 2021; Del Maschio et al., 2022; Stankovic et al., 2022), which show that cognitive and emotional processes shift when we operate in a non-native language.
text.formatted: This idea is supported by studies on the Foreign Language Effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Białek et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Circi et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Del Maschio et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Stankovic et al., 2022)</ref>, which show that cognitive and emotional processes shift when we operate in a non-native language.

text.text: First, using a foreign language dampens our emotional reactions.
This happens because foreign languages are less tied to the emotional experiences and memories that shape how people use and understand their native language (Pavlenko, 2012).
text.formatted: This happens because foreign languages are less tied to the emotional experiences and memories that shape how people use and understand their native language <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Pavlenko, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Because emotions are central to art perception, reduced emotional responses might change it.
Second, using a foreign language distorts our metacognitive ability to track and combine internally produced information.
Thus, thinking in a non-native language can impair reasoning and decision-making (Białek et al., 2020; Białek, 2023).
text.formatted: Thus, thinking in a non-native language can impair reasoning and decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Białek et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Białek, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: If art perception depends on integrating multiple sources of information, such as emotional cues, cultural knowledge, and aesthetic features such as visual form, materials, composition, and sound, then this disruption could alter a piece's perceived meaning or depth.
Finally, comprehension issues may play a role.
When people have limited proficiency in a foreign language, they may struggle to fully understand the linguistic elements of art, such as song lyrics.
This could make finding meaning in what they hear or read harder, lowering their engagement with art.
However, comprehension would not translate into non-verbal artwork, such as paintings or sculptures.
Based on research on the foreign language effect, we speculated that people may perceive art differently when using a foreign language.
To test this hypothesis, we presented participants with art in native and foreign languages.
We focused on two types of art: songs and paintings.
On top of the sensory stimulation that differs between the art forms, they also differ in their reliance on language, as songs include lyrics, and paintings do not.
However, we aim to test the language effect on the profoundness ratings rather than the pure effect of the medium of art.
The paintings still allowed us to study language effects since participants received questions in different languages depending on the experimental condition.
We conducted three experiments (N=345) with different language pairs to test the generalizability of our findings.
All materials (songs and paintings) and data are available at https://osf.io/6aqh4/?view_only=0b48e990d6c54c3ea40a24ec9c3c8049.
text.formatted: All materials (songs and paintings) and data are available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/6aqh4/?view_only=0b48e990d6c54c3ea40a24ec9c3c8049">https://osf.io/6aqh4/?view_only=0b48e990d6c54c3ea40a24ec9c3c8049</ref>.

text.text: We selected abstract paintings because they lack apparent representational content, creating an ideal context to test whether language influences perception when the viewer must construct meaning.
The ambiguity of abstract art provides a stronger test of our hypothesis, as viewers cannot rely on obvious subject matter to determine profoundness.
Songs were selected based on availability in both language versions performed by the same artists, ensuring musical elements remained constant while only language varied.
The songs were piloted to ensure that both language versions were similarly familiar to participants across all experiments.
Experiment 1a was pre-registered: https://aspredicted.org/WSF_SYQ Experiment 2 was pre-registered: https://aspredicted.org/ppc9-248r.pdf
text.formatted: Experiment 1a was pre-registered: <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/WSF_SYQ">https://aspredicted.org/WSF_SYQ</ref> Experiment 2 was pre-registered: <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/ppc9-248r.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/ppc9-248r.pdf</ref>

text.text: The experiments were approved by the ethics committee at the University of XXX.
We operationalized four constructs to capture art perception.
Profoundness measured the cognitive dimension of aesthetic evaluation, specifically perceived depth and meaningfulness (Thömmes & Hübner, 2014; Turpin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Profoundness measured the cognitive dimension of aesthetic evaluation, specifically perceived depth and meaningfulness <ref type="bibr">(Thömmes & Hübner, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Turpin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Liking operationalized the affective dimension of aesthetic response, representing participants' subjective preference and emotional reaction to the artworks (Graf & Landwehr, 2017; Rodway et al., 2016; Sidhu et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Liking operationalized the affective dimension of aesthetic response, representing participants' subjective preference and emotional reaction to the artworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Graf & Landwehr, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Rodway et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Sidhu et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Recommendation measured behavioural intention, reflecting both personal preference and perceived value to others as an indicator of aesthetic quality judgment.

Familiarity was included as a confounding factor known to correlate with aesthetic preference but not representing art quality per se (Leder et al., 2004; Song et al., 2021); research shows that familiarity influences aesthetic judgments independently of the characteristics of the artwork (Song et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Familiarity was included as a confounding factor known to correlate with aesthetic preference but not representing art quality per se <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Leder et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Song et al., 2021)</ref>; research shows that familiarity influences aesthetic judgments independently of the characteristics of the artwork <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Song et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These measures align with theoretical frameworks that distinguish between affective responses and cognitive appraisals as distinct outputs of art perception (Leder et al., 2004; Pelowski et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These measures align with theoretical frameworks that distinguish between affective responses and cognitive appraisals as distinct outputs of art perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Leder et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Pelowski et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Designing the study required some trade-offs.
We did not provide participants with the definition of those constructs allowing them to follow their gut (i.e. ecologically valid interpretation of art).
However, we risk that participants could have differed in how they interpret the questions, negatively affecting the construct validity.
We proposed three hypotheses based on the mechanisms activated when using foreign languages: Hypothesis 1 (H1): Emotional dampening.
If foreign language use dampens emotional reactions, we expect weaker responses to art in the foreign language condition.
This would result in a lower liking of high-quality art and a higher liking of low-quality art because participants would feel less pleasure or displeasure, respectively.
Since emotional responses influence music and visual art, this effect should appear in both mediums.
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Comprehension issues.
If comprehension difficulties drive the effect, we would expect differences only for music, as lyrics require linguistic processing.
Paintings, which do not rely on language, should not be affected by this mechanism.
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Distorted metacognition.

If foreign language use impairs metacognitive integration of information sources, participants may struggle to combine various sources of information, such as colours, techniques, or lyrics, into a coherent interpretation.
This would reduce the salience of a piece's most striking features and affect judgments of both songs and paintings.
This would produce similar effects as H1, meaning we cannot disentangle the two explanations (i.e., cognitive and emotional), but at least we can observe whether they occur.
>Experiment 1a
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Experiment 1a</head>

text.text: We analyzed data from 78 native Polish participants (mean age 25.8 years, range 20-57, 62 female, 16 male).
Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Polish, N=36) or a foreign language (English, N=42).

A total of 161 additional participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=17), hearing or visual impairments (N=3), and "inattentive" responding (N=141).
Participants were classified as "inattentive" if they failed to listen to the entire duration of more than one song.
If a participant did not fully listen to only one song, we kept their other responses, but data for the specific song were excluded.
This led to the exclusion of an additional 28 individual data points.
These criteria were applied to ensure high data quality.
The Experiment was conducted online using the Qualtrics Survey Platform (https://www.qualtrics.com).
text.formatted: The Experiment was conducted online using the Qualtrics Survey Platform (<ref type="url" target="https://www.qualtrics.com">https://www.qualtrics.com</ref>).

text.text: Participants listened to songs from different genres and looked at abstract paintings.
Each song snippet was about one minute long, rather than using complete songs.
This decision was made to balance ecological validity with the practical constraints of online testing.
Our pilot testing indicated that longer song durations significantly decreased completion rates and increased inattentive responding.
Even with these abbreviated excerpts, we still encountered substantial data loss from participants not listening to the full minute.

Participants rated each piece of art on four scales: 1) whether the song or painting was profound (profoundness), 2) whether they liked it (liking), 3) whether they would recommend it (recommendation), and 4) whether they already knew it (familiarity).
Answers were on a scale from 1 ("certainly no") to 7 ("certainly yes").
Each condition had eight songs and eight paintings, but each participant rated only a random sample of four songs and four paintings.
The same paintings were used in both language conditions, with only the language of the questions and answers differing.
All of them were original abstract paintings from the 19th and 20th centuries, presented as digital reproductions.
The songs were the same across conditions and performed by the same artists in their Polish and English versions.
The familiarity scale was included to ensure that any differences between conditions were driven by the foreign language effect and not higher familiarity with Polish song versions.
We have also asked participants to rate paintings on familiarity.
Each song snippet was about one minute long, and participants were instructed to listen to the complete snippet before submitting their ratings.
As far as paintings were concerned, participants could look at them however long they liked.
At the end of the study, participants answered questions about their vision and hearing, age, gender, and English proficiency.
In the preregistration, we planned to average the profoundness, liking, and recommendation ratings into a single composite score called "quality."

However, the internal consistency of these measures was low (ICC = 0.32), which indicates that they capture distinct aspects of artistic evaluation rather than reflecting a single underlying dimension, making it methodologically inappropriate to combine them into a composite score, so we analysed them separately.
We focused primarily on profoundness as it directly relates to the Foreign Language Effect's potential impact on perceived depth and meaning in art, which was our primary research interest.
We ran three mixed models, one for each measure as a dependent variable.
Since we were most interested in profoundness (see Table 1), we report the results with profoundness as the dependent variable here.
text.formatted: Since we were most interested in profoundness (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), we report the results with profoundness as the dependent variable here.

text.text: The analyses for liking and recommendation are in the Supplement, along with the descriptive statistics (Supplement Tables 1 2 3 4 5).
text.formatted: The analyses for liking and recommendation are in the Supplement, along with the descriptive statistics (Supplement Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> <ref type="table">4</ref> <ref type="table">5</ref>).

text.text: Data for this and subsequent experiments were analysed using Jamovi 2.2 (The Jamovi Project, 2021) using Gamlj package (Gallucci, 2019).
text.formatted: Data for this and subsequent experiments were analysed using Jamovi 2.2 (The Jamovi Project, 2021) using Gamlj package <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Gallucci, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The base model (M1) predicted profoundness ratings based on language (English: -0.5, Polish: 0.5) and type of art (paintings: -0.5, music: 0.5).
We clustered the data by the participants' ID and song/painting ID.
Additional models included familiarity with the piece (M2) and English proficiency (M3).
We also tested models accounting for participant sex (M4 -Supplement).

text.text: The base model (M1) showed no significant effects, implying no effect of language on perception of profoundness of the art (H1, H2, and H3 not supported).
Adding familiarity (M2) revealed a significant effect: more familiar pieces were rated as more profound (B=0.19, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35], p<.05).
text.formatted: Adding familiarity (M2) revealed a significant effect: more familiar pieces were rated as more profound (B=0.19, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35], p<.05).

text.text: No other effects were significant.
The proficiency model (M3) found a significant three-way interaction between proficiency, language, and type of art (B=0.40, 95% CI [-0.71, -0.09], p<.05).
text.formatted: The proficiency model (M3) found a significant three-way interaction between proficiency, language, and type of art (B=0.40, 95% CI [-0.71, -0.09], p<.05).

text.text: This interaction suggests that the relationship between language and art type depended on participants' English proficiency (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: This interaction suggests that the relationship between language and art type depended on participants' English proficiency (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The marginal R² values (0.04-0.07) indicate that fixed effects explained only a small portion of the variance.
In other words, our experimental manipulations contributed very little to our ability to predict profoundness ratings. 1a.
We conducted a similar experiment with Dutch as a native language and English as a foreign language to test whether the main effect of language would appear in a different language pair.
We analysed data from 57 native Dutch participants (mean age 21.3 years, range 18-39, 40 female, 17 male).
Depending on their assigned condition, each participant completed the study in their native language (Dutch, N=31) or a foreign language (English, N=26).
Additional 39 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=2), hearing or visual impairments (N=2), and inattentive responding (N=35).
As in Experiment 1a, we excluded data points for items where participants did not listen to the entire snippet.
This led to the exclusion of an additional 8 data points.

Based on the preregistration, we also tested the effect of participant sex (M4 -Supplement).
We conducted a mixed-effects analysis of profoundness ratings.
The base model (M1) showed a significant main effect of type of art (B=0.69, 95% CI [0.06, 1.33], p < .05), with music rated higher than paintings.

text.text: As in Experiment 1a, the marginal R² values were small (0.05-0.08), indicating that fixed effects explained only a small portion of the variance.
In other words, in the best-case scenario all our experimental manipulations predicted 8% of the variance of the profoundness ratings. 1b.
Experiments 1a and 1b tested whether using a foreign language changes how people rate the profoundness of music and paintings.

Both experiments showed no significant main effects of language, suggesting that the Foreign Language Effect does not strongly influence judgments of the profoundness of art (H1, H2, and H3 not supported).
Instead, other factors, such as the type of art and familiarity, seemed to play more prominent roles.
The low marginal R² values in both experiments indicate that much of the variation in profoundness ratings comes from factors not measured in the study.
These may include personal preferences, cultural background, or specific art features.
The finding that music was rated more profound in Experiment 1b points to important differences between the two art forms.
Music often combines multiple elements, such as melody, rhythm, and lyrics, which may evoke emotional responses more directly.
Paintings, especially abstract ones, rely on visual cues and may demand more cognitive effort to interpret.
This main effect of the type of art was not observed in Experiment 1a, which could have depended on the sample, cultural context, or other factors.
In both experiments, familiarity was associated with higher profoundness ratings.
Participants gave higher ratings to pieces of art they recognized, which fits with earlier research showing that people often prefer familiar art (Cutting, 2003).
text.formatted: Participants gave higher ratings to pieces of art they recognized, which fits with earlier research showing that people often prefer familiar art <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cutting, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The three-way interaction between proficiency, language, and type of art found in both experiments shows that individual differences shape how people perceive art.
Proficiency in English mattered more for music than paintings, possibly because music involves linguistic elements.
Observing this three-way interaction prompted us to run another experiment to increase the number of participants.
It was necessary to ensure the robustness of the findings and statistical validity.
The study included both language pairs from Experiments 1a and 1b (Polish-English and Dutch-English).
Paintings were not included in this experiment because we found no significant language effects for paintings in our earlier experiments.

Given our primary interest in the Foreign Language Effect and considering the resource constraints of running large-scale experiments, we focused Experiment 2 exclusively on music, where the linguistic component was more directly relevant and where we had observed more variability in responses.
We analyzed data from N=210 participants (mean age 31.3 years, range 18-75, 88 female, 121 male, 1 other).
Half of the participants were native Dutch speakers (N=109), and the other half were native Polish speakers (N=101).

An additional 35 participants were excluded based on the following criteria: English proficiency below 5 on a scale of 1-10 (N=5), hearing or visual impairments (N=4), and inattentive responding (N=26).
As in the previous experiments, we excluded data points for items where participants did not listen to the entire song, excluding another 13 data points.
Participants were assigned to the version of the experiment corresponding to their language pair (Polish-English or Dutch-English).
They were then randomly assigned to one of the blocks, where half of the songs (4 songs) were in their native language, and the other half were in their foreign language.
This experiment differed from the previous two by excluding paintings as a control variable.
The rest of the materials and the experimental protocol were the same as in the earlier experiments.
We ran an analysis similar to Experiments 1a and 1b.
As before, we ran separate mixed models for different dependent variables due to low internal consistency (ICC=0.36).

text.text: The base model (M1) predicted profoundness ratings based on language (Foreign: -0.5, Native: 0.5).
We clustered the data by the participants' ID and song ID.
Additional models included familiarity with the song (M2) and English proficiency (M3) as control variables.
The base model (M1) showed no significant effects (H1, H2, and H3 not supported).
This means we again failed to observe an effect of language on profoundness ratings.
When controlling for familiarity (M2), we found a significant positive effect of familiarity (B=0.19, 95% CI [0.16, 0.22], p<.001).
text.formatted: When controlling for familiarity (M2), we found a significant positive effect of familiarity (B=0.19, 95% CI [0.16, 0.22], p<.001).

text.text: Participants consistently rated more familiar songs as more profound.
The model replacing familiarity with proficiency (M3) showed no significant effects, indicating that participants' foreign language proficiency did not influence their profoundness ratings.
The clustering in this experiment was stronger than in Experiments 1a and 1b.
As in Experiments 1a and 1b, marginal R² values remained low (0.01-0.07), showing that the fixed effects explained only little variance in profoundness ratings.
As in Experiments 1a and 1b, Experiment 2 tested whether using a foreign language affects how people rate the profoundness of music, focusing on the same language pairs but excluding paintings.

As in the earlier experiments, there was no significant main effect of language (H1, H2, and H3 not supported), suggesting that the Foreign Language Effect does not strongly influence judgments of profoundness and that our sample sizes did not previously cause the lack of effect.
Familiarity had an effect, with participants rating more familiar songs as more profound.
This aligns with earlier research showing familiarity increases positive evaluations (Cutting, 2003).
text.formatted: This aligns with earlier research showing familiarity increases positive evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cutting, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The clustering effects observed in Experiment 2 were stronger than in Experiments 1a and 1b, reflecting greater individual differences and consistent variation between songs.
This indicates that participants' personal preferences and the characteristics of the songs played a significant role in their ratings.

To ensure sufficient statistical power to catch any small, subtle effects that might have been missed and combine all our findings, we conducted a pooled analysis by combining the data from all three experiments.
This study examined whether using a foreign language affects how people perceive the profoundness of music and paintings.

Across three experiments, two language pairs, and a pooled analysis, we found that the language of presentation had no impact on perceived profoundness, liking, or willingness to recommend either music or paintings (H1, H2, and H3 not supported across all experiments).
By pooling data across experiments, we confirmed that the null effect of language was not due to limited statistical power.
Rather than language, familiarity with the art (the greater, the better) and the type of art itself (songs better than paintings) were the only predictors of profoundness ratings we observed.
The consistent influence of familiarity across all experiments shows that it plays a key role in art perception.
Participants rated familiar pieces as more profound, regardless of the language or medium.
This supports earlier findings that people tend to prefer familiar pieces (Cutting, 2003).
text.formatted: This supports earlier findings that people tend to prefer familiar pieces <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cutting, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The type of art also shaped profoundness ratings.
Music was rated as more profound than paintings in Experiments 1a and 1b and when pooled.
Music often engages listeners immediately and requires less interpretation and prior knowledge on the topic to be appreciated.
In contrast, abstract paintings demand more effort and knowledge to interpret, making them more challenging to appreciate (Miu et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In contrast, abstract paintings demand more effort and knowledge to interpret, making them more challenging to appreciate <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Miu et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The consistent finding that music received higher profoundness ratings suggests medium-specific effects warranting further investigation.
Our findings challenge the idea that the Foreign Language Effect significantly influences how people perceive art.
While foreign languages can affect emotions and decision-making in some contexts, these effects seem irrelevant to art perception.
Art perception may involve mechanisms that are not easily changed by linguistic manipulation.
This aligns with our previous work showing that other linguistic manipulations also do not significantly change how people perceive art (e.g., pseudo-profound descriptions, Urbanek et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This aligns with our previous work showing that other linguistic manipulations also do not significantly change how people perceive art (e.g., pseudo-profound descriptions, <ref type="bibr">Urbanek et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The main limitation of our study is that our experimental manipulations explained only a small portion of variance in profoundness ratings, suggesting that unmeasured factors play a substantial role.
These factors could include personal preferences, cultural background, art expertise, or the unique qualities of each piece.
Future research should consider measuring and controlling for such individual differences to better isolate language effects.
Hypothetically, art expertise could be most promising factor explaining the evaluations.
A second limitation concerns our online methodology.
Conducting the study remotely may have dampened participants' emotional engagement with the artworks.
If the online context already reduced emotional responses to a low baseline, the foreign language manipulation may have produced a floor effect, further reducing engagement below detectable levels.
Field studies conducted in naturalistic settings, such as concerts or art exhibitions, might reveal language effects that were obscured in our online paradigm.
Finally, our design created an important asymmetry between the two art forms.
For songs, the foreign language was embedded in the artwork itself (the lyrics), whereas for paintings, the foreign language appeared only in the evaluation context (the questionnaire).

This means our study primarily tested whether evaluating art in a second language affects judgments, rather than whether experiencing linguistically-mediated art in a second language affects perception.

The null result for paintings may simply indicate that reading rating scales in a foreign language does not alter visual perception; a much weaker test of the Foreign Language Effect than we originally intended.
Future research should ensure that the language manipulation is embedded in the aesthetic experience itself, not merely in the evaluation process.
In summary, our findings demonstrate that the language in which people encounter art does not meaningfully shape their aesthetic experience.

Across three experiments with 345 participants, two language pairs, and multiple artistic media, we found no evidence that using a foreign versus native language affects judgments of profoundness, liking, or recommendation.
Instead, aesthetic perception was consistently driven by familiarity with specific artworks and by medium-specific characteristics, with music rated as more profound than paintings.
These results suggest that while the Foreign Language Effect influences moral judgments and decision-making under risk, its impact does not extend to aesthetic domains.

Art perception appears to be governed by stable individual preferences and prior exposure rather than by linguistic context, highlighting the specificity of foreign language effects across different cognitive domains and the robustness of aesthetic preferences across linguistic boundaries.

In contrast, the high conditional R² values (0.43-0.47) show that stable individual preferences (ICC=0.30 for participants) and item characteristics (ICC=0.23 for artworks) dominated profoundness ratings.
Regarding our experimental manipulations, language of presentation had no detectable influence on profoundness ratings.
Instead, those ratings were primarily driven by familiarity with specific artworks and, secondarily, by artistic medium (music vs. painting).
